title: Every line true to the source
statement: Everything a lesson says, quoted or not, from model answers and feedback to marking guides, must be true to its source and claim no more than the source's words support.
example: One marking guide failed a student who gave the source's four pairings and passed one who gave the wrong pairings it named.
detail: A source-fidelity review of the reading course found a model answer that chained two separate consequences into a mechanism the source never states, the same merged mechanism in corrective feedback, feedback that half-conceded a wrong option's claim that an action always works, and a marking guide that failed a student giving the source's four pairings while passing the wrong ones it named. A check of another lesson found five feedback and reveal lines that contradicted the story. The project's protocol for a text's claims about the world holds any text with a failed claim as a draft, since a wrong claim in a child's science text is a kill, not a footnote. What a lesson tells a student includes its model answers and feedback as well as its hints and definitions.
against: A true but unsupported addition was judged less harmful: an example detail invented for a word card, but true of real ecology, was recorded as worth fixing rather than critical (`grade3-reading/artifacts/g5-course/ADVERSARIAL-REVIEW-2026-08-20-R4.md`, line 56). The ruling states it two ways: an inference may only use what the passage's own words show, yet the procedure combines text clues with what you know, so where expected knowledge ends is left to judgment (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0180-lesson-structure-procedure-rulings.qmd`). Where a named design governs, a string it prescribes is not changed even when an audit finds it wrong; a prescribed definition the audit faulted was kept as the design has it, pending a ruling (`grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-live-walk-2026-09-30/BUILD-SPEC.md`; `grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-inceptbench-2026-09-30/REGISTER.md`).
